result.summary: Jove looks away from the battle, and Neptune secretly rallies the Achaeans, inspiring the two Ajaxes and fighting beside Idomeneus. Many warriors fall on both sides, until Polydamas advises Hector to regroup and the Trojans press the attack again.

scenes.title: Neptune Descends to the Ships
scenes.summary: Jove turns his eyes away, and Neptune leaves Samothrace for his palace at Aegae. He drives his chariot over the sea and stables his horses in a cave.
scenes.stakes: Neptune risks the anger of his elder brother Jove by helping the Achaeans.

place.name: Samothrace, Aegae and the cave between Tenedos and Imbrus

scenes.title: Neptune Rouses the Achaeans
scenes.summary: As Calchas, Neptune fills the two Ajaxes with courage, then rebukes the other leaders. The Achaeans form a tight wall, and Hector urges the Trojans on.
scenes.stakes: The Achaeans risk the loss of their ships and destruction by the Trojans.

scenes.title: Teucer Kills Imbrius
scenes.summary: Meriones breaks his spear on Deiphobus's shield. Teucer kills Imbrius, and Hector kills Amphimachus. The Ajaxes seize Imbrius's body, and Neptune plans further mischief.
scenes.stakes: Warriors risk death and the loss of their dead's armour.

scenes.title: Idomeneus and Meriones Arm
scenes.summary: Neptune, as Thoas, spurs Idomeneus, who arms himself and meets Meriones. They go to the left wing as Jove and Neptune pull the war in opposite directions.
scenes.stakes: Idomeneus risks his honour and life if he fails the Achaeans in this crisis.

scenes.title: Fighting on the Left Wing
scenes.summary: Idomeneus kills Othryoneus, Asius and Alcathous, and challenges Deiphobus. Aeneas is called, and many men fall, including Pisander to Menelaus. Paris kills Euchenor.
scenes.stakes: Idomeneus risks death as his strength fails; many warriors risk death.

place.name: The left wing by the ships

scenes.title: Polydamas Counsels Hector
scenes.summary: Hector presses the centre while the Ajaxes hold firm. Polydamas urges caution, Hector rebukes Paris, and he and Ajax trade boasts as the Trojans advance.
scenes.stakes: Hector risks his army being destroyed if he ignores Polydamas, and the Trojans risk disaster at the ships.

place.name: The ships of Ajax and Protesilaus

alias_notes.explanation: Another name for Paris, husband of Helen.

notable_quotes.reason: Neptune's pithy exhortation: the brave recover quickly from setbacks.
Menelaus notes men tire of everything else but never of battle.

analysis.text: Divine intervention shapes the battle, with Neptune defying Jove's plan while fearing his elder brother.
The Locrian archers and slingers contrast with the heavy-armed heroes, reflecting differing fighting styles in the Greek world.

fun_facts.text: The Hippemolgi, 'mare-milkers', named in the opening, are early literary references to nomadic steppe peoples.

language_notes.text: Hippemolgi means 'mare-milkers', a nomadic people imagined at the edge of the known world; the Abians are likewise a distant, idealized people.
'Kept no blind look-out' means Neptune had been watching attentively, unlike Jove, who assumes no god will interfere.
The 'three strides... with the fourth' is a formula of divine speed, showing how vast his steps are.
'Ambrosial forage' is the immortal food of the gods' horses; ambrosia means 'deathless'.
To hobble is to tie an animal's legs so it cannot wander off.
Neptune's epithets: "earth-encircling" refers to the sea thought to surround the land; "lord of the earthquake" marks him as the shaker of the earth. He is the Greek Poseidon.
"Swift Ajax son of Oileus" is the lesser Ajax, distinguished from Ajax son of Telamon, the greater Ajax.
"Soon recognised" means gods are easily recognised, here by the way their feet and knees look or move as they depart.
"Hinds" are female deer; "portent" is an omen, here an alarming sign of how the war has turned.
The sense is that even Mars or Minerva could not scorn or find fault with these picked men if they came among them.
"Spouse of Juno" means Jove (Zeus), whose favour Hector hopes he has; "swords and spears pointed at both ends" describes double-pointed spears.
"Orb of ox-hide" is a poetic phrase for the round shield, which was made of layered bull hides.
"To wit" is an archaic phrase meaning "that is to say" or "namely."
"Ilius" is Ilium, i.e. Troy. "Danaan" and "Achaeans" both mean the Greeks.
"Bronze-dight" means adorned or equipped with bronze; "dight" is archaic for arrayed.
"Son of Oileus" is the lesser Ajax, distinguished from Ajax son of Telamon.
Neptune (the Greek Poseidon) is Amphimachus's grandfather; the text gives no further detail here, so his anger is personal as well as partisan.
"None are held back neither by fear nor slackness" is a double negative; the sense is that no one is held back by fear or slackness.
"Batten upon" means to feed greedily on; the curse is that the slacker's corpse be eaten by dogs.
"Squire" here means a attendant-warrior who serves a chief in battle; Meriones is also a fighter.
"Bossed shields" are shields with raised metal studs at the centre; "corslets" are body armour.
Thrace, the Ephyri and the Phlegyans are warlike peoples and places linked with Mars; the simile says he may pass over them to join this battle.
Fire on the ships is the Trojans' goal; burning them would strand the Achaeans, so only Jove's own hand could make Hector succeed.
Jove had promised Thetis to honour her son Achilles by letting the Trojans prevail while Achilles stays out of the fighting.
The "knot of war" is a metaphor for a deadlock that neither side can break, with both armies pulling.
"Gifts of wooing" are the bride-price a suitor paid the bride's family; Othryoneus offers military service instead. "To wit" means "that is to say."
Idomeneus speaks in bitter mockery: he feigns admiration while taunting the dying man. "Vaunted" means boasted or gloated.
"Esquire" here means the charioteer, the attendant who drives the chariot while the warrior fights on foot.
Hades' house is the underworld; Deiphobus jokes that Asius will have a slain man as escort into it.
Neptune (the Greek Poseidon) favours the Achaeans here, so he paralyses Alcathous so that Idomeneus can kill him.
"Mars" is the Roman name for Ares, god of war, here standing for death in battle.
"Jove-begotten" means descended from Jove (the Greek Zeus); Idomeneus traces his line through Minos, a son of Jove.
Aeneas' grievance is that Priam did not honour him properly, though he was of the royal house.
"Death, life's foe" is a Homeric formula for death; "shed around him" means it poured over him like a mist.
Neptune (the Greek Poseidon) is secretly helping the Achaeans in this book, which is why Antilochus's body is protected.
"Pulse" means dried peas or beans; the winnowing-shovel tossed grain into the wind to separate chaff.
"Esquire" here means the attendant who carries a warrior's gear.
"Vaunted" means boasted triumphantly over a fallen enemy.
Refers to Paris's abduction of Helen, Menelaus's wife, and treasure while Paris was a guest in his house; Jove protected guest-right.
Euchenor chose war to avoid the fine Achaeans imposed on men who stayed home; the prophecy gave him two fates to choose between.
Neptune (the Greek Poseidon) is secretly helping the Achaeans; 'ere long' means 'before long'.
These are contingents named by homeland: Boeotians, Ionians, Locrians, Phthians and Epeans, each fighting under its own leaders.
'Swart' means dark; 'fallow field' is land ploughed but left unsown for a season.
The Locrians fight as light-armed archers and slingers, not as heavily armoured spearmen, so they cannot stand in close combat.
'Debt of yesterday' refers to the Trojans' earlier success; the one 'never weary of battle' is Achilles, who is still out of the fighting.
'Scatheless' means unharmed; 'sterns' are the rear ends of the ships drawn up on shore.
'Woman-mad' alludes to Paris abducting Helen, which caused the war.
Alexandrus is another name for Paris.
Saturn's son is Jove (Zeus).
A bird on the right was a favourable omen in Greek belief; the Achaeans take it as a sign of success.
Hector says he is as certain of destroying the Achaeans as he would wish to be certain of being a god's son.

context_notes.text: Samothrace is a mountainous island in the north Aegean; from its peak Neptune (the Greek Poseidon) can see Troy and Mount Ida.
Aegae is Neptune's underwater palace home, here placed in the depths of the sea.
Tenedos and Imbrus are islands near the Trojan coast, so the cave lies close to the Greek camp.
Calchas was the Greek army's seer, who interpreted omens. Neptune takes his form so the Achaeans will trust the encouragement.
Agamemnon had insulted Achilles (son of Peleus) by taking his prize, so Achilles withdrew from the fighting.
Hector has broken through the gates of the Achaean wall, an important turning point in the battle.
Imbrius's wife was a daughter of Priam born outside marriage, so he was a son-in-law of the Trojan king and highly honoured.
Neptune often takes a mortal's form to speak to heroes. Here he disguises himself as Thoas, an Aetolian leader, to rouse Idomeneus.
Neptune, god of the sea and earthquakes, has taken the form of Thoas, an Achaean leader, to rally the Greeks secretly.
Idomeneus is king of the Cretans and one of the senior Achaean commanders.
An ambush was considered a true test of courage, since men had to wait silently and still, with nothing to distract them from fear.
Jove and Neptune are brothers, sons of Saturn; Jove, the elder, is the supreme god, so Neptune avoids openly defying him.
Idomeneus is the elderly king of Crete and one of the leading Achaean (Danaan) warriors.
Cassandra was Priam's prophetic daughter, doomed never to be believed.
Alcathous was married to Aeneas' sister, which is why Deiphobus appeals to family ties.
Jove had forbidden the gods to join the fighting, so Mars sits on Olympus ignorant of his son's death.
Polites and Deiphobus are sons of King Priam, so they are Paris's brothers.
Helenus is another son of Priam and was a seer; Thracian swords were prized foreign weapons.
The Paphlagonians were allies of Troy from northern Asia Minor, led by Pylaemenes.
Paris had been Harpalion's guest, so guest-friendship obliges him to avenge the death.
Medon, a bastard half-brother of the lesser Ajax, lives in exile at Phylace after killing a kinsman, a common reason for leaving one's homeland.
Polydamas is a Trojan commander who repeatedly gives Hector cautious advice that Hector often rejects.
Mars (the Greek Ares) is the god of war.

literary_notes.text: Jove believes no god will intervene, but the reader has just been told Neptune is watching and about to act.
Hills and forests quaking under his feet conveys the overwhelming power of the god.
The sea rejoices and opens a path, treating Neptune as a beloved lord recognized by his realm.
The axle staying dry exaggerates the horses' speed, skimming the waves.
The Trojans' advance is compared to a storm-cloud and flame, suggesting overwhelming, destructive force.
Neptune's sudden departure is compared to a falcon swooping from a height, conveying swift, effortless divine movement.
Ajax's words reveal the disguise failed only as the god left; gods are recognised only when it is too late to question them.
The repeated "to" phrases (spear to spear, shield to shield) build the picture of an unbroken wall of men.
Hector is likened to a rolling boulder that rushes until stopped on level ground, foreshadowing that his charge will be checked.
Imbrius's fall is compared to a felled ash-tree on a mountain, conveying his height, his dignity and the finality of his collapse.
The Ajaxes are likened to lions stealing a goat from hounds, showing their ferocity and their snatching of the body from the Trojans.
The head sent whirling like a ball is a grim, vivid image of brutality, and it pointedly lands at Hector's feet.
Idomeneus' gleaming armour is compared to Jove's lightning, a sign to mortals, suggesting his divine-seeming power as he rushes to battle.
A long digression on the coward's body and the brave man's calm defines courage through physical detail and praises Meriones.
Meriones and Idomeneus are likened to Mars and his son Panic, casting them as terrifying war-spirits.
The fury of the fight is compared to dust-laden winds, conveying a blinding, chaotic storm.
"Iron indeed must be his courage" compares steadfastness to metal and shows the narrator addressing the audience directly.
The knot of war pulled by two gods shows the battle as a tug-of-war, and men's knees fail beneath the strain.
Othryoneus promises to drive out the Achaeans as a bride-price, a boast that leads straight to his death.
Asius' fall is compared to a felled tree cut for shipbuilding, making the death vast and linking the war to ordinary labour.
Idomeneus is likened to a boar at bay, showing fierce, defiant courage despite his age.
Aeneas' followers are compared to sheep following a ram, with the pleased shepherd mirroring Aeneas' gladness.
Idomeneus' failing strength and slow retreat show his age and the limits of an otherwise formidable hero.
Meriones is compared to a vulture, stressing his swift, predatory strike and retreat.
The dying Adamas writhing on the spear is likened to a bound bull dragged by herdsmen, making his helpless pain vivid.
The arrow bouncing off the shield is compared to beans leaping off a winnowing shovel, an everyday farm image set in battle.
The narrator tells us Pisander's doom before the fight, with a direct address to Menelaus.
Menelaus addresses Jove directly, complaining about the god's apparent favouring of the Trojans.
The battle is likened to a flaming fire, closing the scene with an image of spreading destruction.
Hector is 'a wall of fire', conveying his unstoppable, destructive force against the Greek defenders.
The two Ajaxes are compared to oxen pulling a plough, showing their steady joint effort and closeness.
Hector towering 'like a snowy mountain' suggests his size, brightness and imposing presence.
The Trojan ranks are compared to storm winds and waves rolling in, conveying their relentless, wave-after-wave advance.
Hector's wish to be a god's son, equal to Minerva and Apollo, exaggerates his confidence in victory; it is also ironic given his fate.
